standard_text: Give examples of rational and irrational numbers and explain the difference; understand that every number has a decimal expansion -- rational numbers have expansions that terminate or eventually repeat, and convert a repeating decimal expansion to a fraction.

progression.narrative:
This standard braids two ideas: SORT numbers into rational and irrational, and understand the DECIMAL EXPANSION that decides which pile a number lands in. Everything rests on one definition -- a rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers, and its decimal either terminates or eventually repeats; an irrational number cannot, so its decimal runs on forever with no repeating block. The progression opens where recognition lives: picking the irrational numbers out of an easy set (√2, √3, π) and, crucially, learning that a repeating decimal like 0.333... is rational even though it never ends. It then widens to classifying square roots, where the trap flips -- √25 is rational because 25 is a perfect square, while √7 is irrational.

The second strand makes the decimal expansion concrete and reversible. Students convert a fraction to its decimal and decide whether it terminates or repeats (a denominator of only 2s and 5s terminates; any other factor repeats), then run the machine backward -- converting a repeating decimal into a fraction by setting it equal to x, shifting, and subtracting so the endless tail cancels (0.4545... = 45/99 = 5/11). The two strands meet in an At-proficiency task that asks students to find the single genuine irrational among tricky look-alikes, and the capstone reasons about the number system itself: judging and justifying claims such as 'every repeating decimal is irrational' (false) with a definition or a counterexample. The through-line we keep naming: rational means it can be a fraction, so its decimal terminates or repeats; irrational means it cannot, so its decimal never terminates and never repeats. No calculator is allowed, so every square root, fraction, and decimal is one students can reason about by hand.

steps.rationale: The Below-proficiency entry point and the standard's first demand: give examples of irrational numbers and separate them from rationals, learning that a repeating decimal never ends yet is still rational.
Extends classification to square roots, where the rational/irrational split hinges on whether the radicand is a perfect square -- the discrimination the standard's 'explain the difference' demands.
The decimal-expansion demand in the forward direction: show that a rational number's decimal terminates or repeats by converting the fraction and classifying the result.
The standard's named skill -- convert a repeating decimal expansion into a fraction -- running the decimal expansion backward with the set-equal-to-x-and-subtract method.
The At-proficiency synthesis: find the one genuine irrational among tricky look-alikes, forcing students to test radicands and repeats rather than trust surface cues.
The Above-proficiency reasoning (DOK 3): analyze and justify a generalization about rational and irrational numbers with a definition or a counterexample.

skills.name: Convert a fraction to a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator

prerequisite_skill.description: Divide the numerator by the denominator to write a fraction as a decimal.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 3/4 written as a decimal?

skills.i_do_script: A fraction is a division problem: the bar means 'divide the top by the bottom.' Watch: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4 = 0.75, and 1/8 means 1 divided by 8 = 0.125. I keep the common ones in my head -- 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/8 = 0.125. Being able to divide a fraction into a decimal is what later lets me see whether that decimal terminates or repeats.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the denominator by the numerator, or reads the fraction bar backward
canonical_error.example: Writes 1/4 as 4.0 (dividing 4 by 1) or 0.4 instead of 0.25
canonical_error.why: The student divides the larger number by the smaller, or forgets the bar means top-divided-by-bottom. a/b always means a divided by b, not b divided by a.

skills.item_template: A simple fraction to convert to a decimal. Short response fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: The bar means top divided by bottom.
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite the fraction as a division: 3/4 is 3 divided by 4. Put a decimal point and zeros on the top, then divide.
redirect_script.praise: You divided the numerator by the denominator -- that's the decimal.

vocabulary.definition: The top number of a fraction; it tells how many parts you have.
The bottom number of a fraction; it tells how many equal parts make one whole.

worked_example_script.text: Write 3/8 and read it as '3 divided by 8.'
Put a decimal point and zeros after the 3. What is 3.000 divided by 8?
3 divided by 8 = 0.375. The fraction bar just means divide the top by the bottom.
If a student writes 2.67 (8 divided by 3), ask 'which number goes inside the division box, the top or the bottom?'
Your turn: write 1/4 as a decimal.

skills.name: Identify whether a whole number is a perfect square and name its square root

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize a perfect square and state its whole-number square root.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Is 25 a perfect square, and what is its square root?

skills.i_do_script: A perfect square is a whole number that equals some whole number times itself, so its square root is a whole number. Watch: 25 = 5 x 5, so √25 = 5, a whole number. But 20 is not a perfect square -- 4 x 4 = 16 and 5 x 5 = 25, and nothing whole squares to 20, so √20 is not a whole number. Knowing which numbers are perfect squares is what lets me decide whether a square root is a tidy rational number or not.

canonical_error.pattern: Assumes every square root is a whole number, or that any number under a root is a perfect square
canonical_error.example: Says √20 = 10 (half of 20) or treats √20 as a whole number, instead of recognizing 20 is not a perfect square
canonical_error.why: The student expects a radical to always simplify to a whole number. Only the square root of a perfect square (like 25) is a whole number; the root of a non-perfect-square (like 20) is not.

skills.item_template: A whole number; student states whether it is a perfect square and its root. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Is 16 a perfect square? What is its square root?
Is 36 a perfect square? What is its square root?

redirect_script.stop: Is there a whole number that squares to it?
redirect_script.prompt: Test the number against your square facts (4, 9, 16, 25, 36...). If no whole number times itself lands exactly on it, its square root is not a whole number.
redirect_script.praise: You checked for an exact whole-number root -- that's a perfect square.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 36 = 6 x 6.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; √25 = 5.

next_steps.if_fail: Review square roots of perfect squares (7.NS.6).

worked_example_script.text: Write 49 and 50 side by side.
Is there a whole number that times itself gives 49? What about 50?
7 x 7 = 49, so 49 is a perfect square and √49 = 7. Nothing whole squares to 50, so √50 is not a whole number.
If a student says √50 = 25, ask 'does 25 times 25 equal 50, or did you just halve it?'
Your turn: is 64 a perfect square, and what is its root?

skills.name: Identify which numbers in a set are irrational
skills.i_do_script: An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers, and its decimal goes on forever WITHOUT repeating. The easy irrationals to know are √2, √3, and π. Watch this set: √2, 0.333..., 7, √16. √2 is irrational -- 2 is not a perfect square. But 0.333... repeats (it equals 1/3), 7 is an integer, and √16 = 4, so those three are rational. The trap is thinking a decimal that 'never ends' must be irrational -- a repeating decimal never ends but is still rational.

canonical_error.pattern: Marks a repeating decimal as irrational because it 'never ends'
canonical_error.example: Selects 0.333... as irrational, when 0.333... = 1/3 is rational
canonical_error.why: The student equates 'endless decimal' with irrational. Only a decimal that is BOTH non-terminating AND non-repeating is irrational; a repeating decimal like 0.333... is rational because it equals a fraction.

skills.item_template: A set of numbers; student selects all that are irrational. Multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Select all numbers that are irrational: √2, 0.5, 0.333..., π, √25
sample_items.distractor_logic: √2 and π are irrational. 0.5 terminates, 0.333... = 1/3 repeats, √25 = 5 -- all rational.

sample_items.answer: Irrational (3 is not a perfect square)
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 is not a perfect square, so √3 is non-terminating and non-repeating.
A repeating decimal equals a fraction of integers.
√5 and π are irrational; 4/9 and 0.25 are rational.

redirect_script.stop: Does it repeat, or truly never repeat?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask two questions: can it be written as a fraction? does its decimal repeat? If it repeats (like 0.333...), it is rational. Only √2, √3, π and endless non-repeating decimals are irrational.
redirect_script.praise: You separated 'endless but repeating' from truly irrational -- exactly right.

vocabulary.definition: A number that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers; its decimal never ends and never repeats, like √2 or π.
A number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, like 3/4, 7, or 0.333... = 1/3.

worked_example_script.text: Write the set: √2, 0.5, 0.333..., π.
Which of these cannot be written as a fraction and never repeats?
√2 and π are irrational; 0.5 = 1/2 and 0.333... = 1/3 are rational.
If a student picks 0.333..., ask 'does it repeat? what fraction does it equal?'
Your turn: is √5 rational or irrational?

practice_problems.stem: Is √2 rational or irrational?
Is 1/2 rational or irrational?
Select all irrational numbers: √2, 0.333..., π, √16
Is 0.111... rational or irrational? Explain.
Jordan sorted some numbers. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Jordan wrote: '0.444... is irrational because the digits go on forever.'
practice_problems.answer: 0.444... repeats (it equals 4/9), so it is rational. A number is irrational only if its decimal never ends AND never repeats.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: endless mistaken for irrational.

practice_problems.stem: Which of these is irrational: √36, √7, 0.8?
Write one rational and one irrational number whose decimals both run past three places.
practice_problems.notes: Produce your own of each type.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why 0.272727... is rational even though it never ends.
practice_problems.answer: It repeats the block 27 forever, so it equals a fraction (3/11); irrational numbers never repeat.

activities.instructions:

2. Sort each card into 'Rational' or 'Irrational.'
3. To place a card in 'Rational,' name the fraction it equals or say why (terminates, repeats, or a perfect-square root).
4. Debrief: why does a repeating decimal like 0.333... belong in the Rational pile?

activities.instructions:

2. Ask: does 0.444... repeat? What fraction does it equal?
3. State whether 0.444... is rational or irrational and why.
4. Write the one test that decides it: does the decimal repeat, or never repeat?

content.error_step: Jordan used 'goes on forever' instead of checking whether the decimal repeats.
content.why: 0.444... repeats and equals 4/9, so it is rational; only a non-repeating, non-terminating decimal is irrational.

activities.title: Rational or Irrational Flash
materials: Number flash cards (mix of √2, π, fractions, repeating and terminating decimals, perfect-square roots)
activities.instructions:

2. Partner B calls 'rational' with a reason (a fraction, terminates, or repeats) or 'irrational.'

The 'endless means irrational' bug is a precise error a quick find-and-fix corrects.

misconception_redirects.say: Ask two questions: can it be written as a fraction? does its decimal repeat? If it repeats (like 0.333...), it is rational. Only √2, √3, π and endless non-repeating decimals are irrational.
misconception_redirects.praise: You separated 'endless but repeating' from truly irrational -- exactly right.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student marks every square root as irrational.
misconception_redirects.say: √25 = 5 and √16 = 4 are rational. A root is irrational only when the number inside is not a perfect square.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the radicand instead of the root sign -- that's the test.

Rational (= 3). 'Irrational' means the student judged by the root sign.

It repeats, so it equals a fraction -- rational.

π is the classic non-repeating, non-terminating decimal.

skills.name: Classify each number as rational or irrational, including square roots
skills.i_do_script: To classify a number I test whether it can be a fraction of integers. Square roots need care: the root of a perfect square is rational (√25 = 5), but the root of a number that is NOT a perfect square is irrational (√7). Watch: √7 -- 7 is not a perfect square, so irrational. √25 = 5, rational. 3/8 is a fraction of integers, rational. 0.2727... repeats, so rational (it equals 3/11). I check each number one at a time against the definition.

canonical_error.pattern: Classifies every square root as irrational, ignoring whether the radicand is a perfect square
canonical_error.example: Labels √25 irrational because it 'has a root sign,' instead of rational (√25 = 5)
canonical_error.why: The student sees the radical and assumes irrational. The square root of a perfect square is a whole number, which is rational; only roots of non-perfect-squares are irrational.

skills.item_template: A table of numbers; student marks each Rational or Irrational. Table match.

sample_items.stem: Classify each as rational or irrational: √7, √25, 3/8, 0.2727...
sample_items.distractor_logic: √7 irrational (7 not a perfect square); √25 = 5; 3/8 is a ratio; 0.2727... = 3/11.

sample_items.answer: Irrational (11 is not a perfect square)

redirect_script.stop: Is the number under the root a perfect square?
redirect_script.prompt: For a square root, check the radicand: if it is a perfect square (like 25), the root is rational; if not (like 7), it is irrational. Don't judge by the root sign alone.
redirect_script.praise: You tested whether the radicand was a perfect square -- that's how to classify a root.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 36 = 6 x 6.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; √25 = 5.

worked_example_script.text: Write √7 and √25 side by side.
Is the number under each root a perfect square?
25 is (√25 = 5, rational); 7 is not (√7 is irrational).
If a student calls √25 irrational, ask 'what whole number squares to 25?'
Your turn: classify √49 and √11.

Is √64 rational or irrational? Explain.

shown_work: Sam wrote: '√81 is irrational because it has a square-root sign.'
practice_problems.answer: √81 = 9, a whole number, so it is rational. A root is irrational only when the number inside is NOT a perfect square.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: root sign mistaken for irrational.

practice_problems.stem: Which is irrational: √16, √17, or √100?
Write two square roots between 10 and 30, one rational and one irrational.
Explain why √9 is rational but √10 is irrational.
practice_problems.answer: 9 is a perfect square (√9 = 3 = 3/1), but 10 is not, so √10 never terminates or repeats.

content.why: 81 is a perfect square, √81 = 9, so it is rational.

misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized the repeat and named the fraction -- that's rational.

quick_checks.look_for: √25 rational, √7 irrational. Calling √25 irrational means judging by the sign.
Irrational (50 is not a perfect square). 'Rational' means they assumed a whole-number root.

√___ is irrational because ___ is not a perfect square.

Any fraction of integers is rational.

skills.name: Convert a fraction to its decimal expansion and classify it as terminating or repeating
skills.i_do_script: Every fraction becomes either a terminating decimal (it stops) or a repeating decimal (a digit or block repeats forever) -- and both are rational. I divide to find the decimal, then classify. Watch: 3/8 = 0.375, which stops, so terminating. 1/6 = 0.1666..., where the 6 repeats forever, so repeating. A shortcut: if the denominator in lowest terms has only 2s and 5s as factors, it terminates; any other factor (like the 3 in 1/6) makes it repeat.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges terminating vs repeating by the size or evenness of the denominator instead of dividing or checking its prime factors
canonical_error.example: Predicts 7/8 repeats because 8 is bigger than 7, when 7/8 = 0.875 terminates; or calls 1/6 terminating because 6 is even
canonical_error.why: The student uses a surface feature. Only fractions whose lowest-terms denominator has just 2 and 5 as prime factors terminate; a factor like 3 (as in 1/6) makes the decimal repeat.

skills.item_template: A set of fractions; student converts each to a decimal and marks terminating or repeating. Table match.

sample_items.stem: Convert each to a decimal and classify: 7/8, 1/3, 2/5, 1/6
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8 = 2^3 and 5 have only 2s/5s (terminate); 3 and 6 = 2 x 3 carry a factor of 3 (repeat).

sample_items.stem: Is 1/4 terminating or repeating? Give the decimal.
Is 5/6 terminating or repeating? Give the decimal.

redirect_script.stop: Divide it out -- don't guess from the size.
redirect_script.prompt: Carry out the division, or factor the denominator: only 2s and 5s make it terminate. 1/6 has a factor of 3, so it repeats; 7/8 is all 2s, so it stops.
redirect_script.praise: You used the denominator's factors (or the division) -- that's how you tell terminating from repeating.

vocabulary.definition: A decimal that stops after a finite number of digits, like 0.875.
A decimal with a digit or block that repeats forever, like 0.1666...

worked_example_script.text: Write 7/8 and 1/6.
Factor each denominator -- only 2s and 5s, or something else?
8 = 2 x 2 x 2, so 7/8 = 0.875 terminates; 6 = 2 x 3, so 1/6 = 0.1666... repeats.
If a student says 7/8 repeats, ask 'what are the prime factors of 8?'
Your turn: does 3/8 terminate or repeat?

practice_problems.stem: What is 1/2 as a decimal? Terminating or repeating?
What is 1/3 as a decimal? Terminating or repeating?
Convert and classify: 7/8, 1/3, 2/5, 1/6
Is 3/8 terminating or repeating? Show the decimal.
Nia classified a fraction. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Nia wrote: '7/8 is repeating because 8 does not divide 7 evenly.'
practice_problems.answer: 7/8 = 0.875, which terminates. A fraction terminates when its denominator has only 2s and 5s -- 8 = 2 x 2 x 2, so 7/8 stops.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: guessing from the denominator's size.

practice_problems.stem: Is 5/6 terminating or repeating?

practice_problems.answer: Terminating -- 20 = 2 x 2 x 5 has only 2s and 5s (9/20 = 0.45).

skills.name: Convert a repeating decimal to a fraction
skills.i_do_script: To turn a repeating decimal into a fraction I set it equal to x, multiply so the repeating part lines up, and subtract. Watch 0.4545...: let x = 0.4545...; the block '45' is 2 digits, so 100x = 45.4545...; subtract x to cancel the endless tail: 100x - x = 45, so 99x = 45, and x = 45/99 = 5/11. The key: a 1-digit block goes over 9, a 2-digit block over 99, a 3-digit block over 999 -- then simplify.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the repeating block over a power of 10 (like a terminating decimal) instead of over 9, 99, or 999
canonical_error.why: The student uses place value (over 100) as if the decimal stopped. A repeating block of length n goes over 10^n - 1 (9, 99, 999) because subtracting x cancels the endless tail.

skills.item_template: A repeating decimal with a 1- or 2-digit block. Student writes it as a fraction. Numeric response.

redirect_script.stop: Over 9s, not over a power of 10.
redirect_script.prompt: Count the repeating digits: 1 digit goes over 9, 2 digits over 99. 0.4545... = 45/99 = 5/11. Then simplify.
redirect_script.praise: You put the block over the right string of 9s and simplified -- that's the method.

vocabulary.definition: A decimal with a digit or block that repeats forever, like 0.4545...
A number written as a ratio of two integers, a/b, like 5/11.

worked_example_script.text: How many digits are in the repeating block? What do we multiply by?
If a student writes 45/100, ask 'did the decimal stop, or repeat forever?'
Your turn: write 0.2727... as a fraction.

1. Read Devon's claim that 0.2727... = 27/100.

3. Write what 99x equals, then solve for x and simplify.
4. Explain why the block goes over 99, not 100.

content.worked_problem: Convert 0.2727... to a fraction. Devon wrote 27/100.
content.error_step: Devon put the repeating block over 100 as if the decimal stopped.

activities.title: Nine-Nines Race
materials: Flash cards of repeating decimals (1- and 2-digit blocks)
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a repeating-decimal card and start the round.
2. Players race to write the fraction: block over the matching 9s, then simplify.
3. First correct and simplified keeps the card.
4. Debrief: which conversions still need the full set-up-and-subtract steps?

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud the set-equal-to-x-and-subtract steps models the whole conversion.
Gradual release from teacher-shown steps to student-run conversions builds independence.
Putting the block over 100 instead of 99 is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects.

questioning_prompts: How many digits are in the repeating block?
What do you multiply x by to line up the tails?
What does subtracting x leave on each side?
Does the block go over a power of 10, or over 9s?
Can the fraction be simplified?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the repeating block over a power of 10 instead of over 9, 99, or 999.
misconception_redirects.say: Count the repeating digits: 1 digit goes over 9, 2 digits over 99. 0.4545... = 45/99 = 5/11. Then simplify.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the block over the right string of 9s and simplified -- that's the method.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds 99x = 45 but forgets to simplify 45/99.
misconception_redirects.say: Good -- now simplify: 45 and 99 share a factor of 9, so 45/99 = 5/11.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reduced the fraction to lowest terms -- that finishes the job.

quick_checks.look_for: 1/3. An answer of 3/10 or 33/100 means the block was put over a power of 10.
5/11. 45/100 diagnoses the power-of-10 error; 45/99 unsimplified is close but not finished.

sentence_starters: The block ___ has ___ digits, so it goes over ___.

steps.annotation: Shift so the endless tails line up.
Subtract x from 100x -- what does 99x equal?
Solve for x and simplify the fraction.

skills.name: Identify the irrational number among numbers that look similar
skills.i_do_script: When several numbers look exotic, I find the ONE that is truly irrational by testing each. Watch: √8, √9, 0.2727..., 5/6. √8 -- 8 is not a perfect square, so irrational. √9 = 3 (rational), 0.2727... repeats = 3/11 (rational), 5/6 is a fraction (rational). So √8 is the irrational one. A radical sign or an endless-looking decimal does NOT by itself mean irrational -- I check whether the radicand is a perfect square and whether the decimal repeats.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats a radical sign or an endless-looking decimal as automatically irrational, without testing the radicand or the repeat
canonical_error.example: For √8, √9, 0.2727..., 5/6 picks √9 (has a root sign) or 0.2727... (never ends) instead of √8
canonical_error.why: The student uses surface cues -- a radical or a long decimal -- instead of testing whether the radicand is a perfect square and whether the decimal repeats. √9 = 3 and 0.2727... = 3/11 are rational; √8 is irrational because 8 is not a perfect square.

skills.item_template: Four tricky options; student selects the single irrational number. Multiple choice.

sample_items.distractor_logic: √8 irrational (8 not a perfect square); √9 = 3; 0.2727... = 3/11; 5/6 rational.

redirect_script.stop: Test each one -- don't trust the symbol.
redirect_script.prompt: For each choice ask: is the number under the root a perfect square? does the decimal repeat? Only the root of a non-perfect-square (like √8) is irrational; √9 and 0.2727... are rational.
redirect_script.praise: You tested each option instead of guessing by the symbol -- that's how you find the irrational one.

vocabulary.definition: A number that cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal never ends and never repeats, like √8 or π.
A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 9 = 3 x 3, whose root is rational.

worked_example_script.text: Write the choices: √8, √9, 0.2727..., 5/6.
Test each: is the radicand a perfect square? does the decimal repeat?
√9 = 3, 0.2727... = 3/11, and 5/6 are rational; √8 is irrational.
If a student picks 0.2727..., ask 'does it repeat? what fraction is it?'
Your turn: which is irrational -- √18, √16, 0.4545..., or 7/12?

practice_problems.stem: Is √9 rational or irrational?
Is √8 rational or irrational?
Which is irrational: √8, √9, 0.2727..., 5/6?
Which is irrational: 0.4545..., √18, √16, 7/12?

practice_problems.answer: 0.4545... repeats (it equals 5/11), so it is rational. The irrational choice is √18, because 18 is not a perfect square.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: 'never ends' instead of 'never repeats.'

practice_problems.stem: Which is irrational: √12, √25, 0.111..., 3/7?
Write four numbers where exactly one is irrational, and name it.
Explain why √16 is rational but √17 is irrational.
practice_problems.answer: 16 is a perfect square (√16 = 4), but 17 is not, so √17 never terminates or repeats.

activities.title: Irrational or Just Looks Like It
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Irrational' or 'Rational (looks tricky).'
2. For a root, check if the radicand is a perfect square; for a decimal, check if it repeats.
3. Name the fraction for each rational card.
4. Debrief: which surface cue -- a root sign or a long decimal -- fooled you more?

activities.title: Never-Ending Isn't Irrational
activities.instructions:
1. Read Priya's claim that 0.454545... is the irrational one because it never ends.
2. Ask: does 0.4545... repeat? What fraction does it equal?
3. Test the other choices and name the real irrational number.
4. Write the difference between 'never ends' and 'never repeats.'

content.error_step: Priya used 'never ends' instead of 'never repeats.'
content.why: 0.4545... = 5/11 is rational; √18 is irrational because 18 is not a perfect square.

activities.title: Spot the Irrational
materials: Sets of four number cards posted around the room
activities.instructions:
1. Post a set of four numbers at each station.
2. Students walk to the one number they believe is irrational.
3. On a signal, each group defends its pick by testing the radicand or the repeat.
4. Debrief: which rational look-alikes drew people in, and why?

strategy_links.why: Contrasting a rational look-alike with the true irrational is exactly a worked-example-plus-error study.
Judging by a root sign or a long decimal is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects.
Number-talk reasoning about testing each option trains verification over surface cues.

questioning_prompts: Is the number under each root a perfect square?
Does each decimal repeat, so equal a fraction?
Why isn't 0.2727... the irrational one?
Which choice is a root of a non-perfect-square?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats a radical or an endless-looking decimal as automatically irrational.
misconception_redirects.say: For each choice ask: is the number under the root a perfect square? does the decimal repeat? Only the root of a non-perfect-square (like √8) is irrational; √9 and 0.2727... are rational.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested each option instead of guessing by the symbol -- that's how you find the irrational one.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks a perfect-square root because it has a radical.
misconception_redirects.say: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4 are whole numbers, so they're rational. The irrational one has a non-perfect-square inside.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the radicand and rejected the tidy root -- exactly right.

quick_checks.look_for: √12. Picking 0.111... shows 'endless' mistaken for irrational; picking √25 shows judging by the sign.

sentence_starters: I tested ___: it is rational because ___.
___ is the irrational one because ___ is not a perfect square.

skills.name: Analyze and justify a generalization about rational and irrational numbers
skills.i_do_script: At this level I judge a claim about rational and irrational numbers and JUSTIFY it -- with a definition or a counterexample. Watch the claim 'every repeating decimal is irrational.' It is false: 0.4545... repeats but equals 5/11, a fraction, so it is rational. To justify, I lean on the definitions: rational = can be written as a fraction (its decimal terminates or repeats); irrational = non-terminating AND non-repeating. One counterexample is enough to disprove an 'always' claim.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies a surface rule ('endless means irrational,' 'irrational times irrational is irrational') instead of testing with the definition or a counterexample
canonical_error.example: Agrees that √2 x √2 is irrational, when √2 x √2 = 2 is rational; or calls 0.4545... irrational because it repeats
canonical_error.why: The student generalizes from appearance rather than the definition. A repeating decimal is rational, and two irrationals can multiply to a rational (√2 x √2 = 2), so 'always' claims must be tested, not assumed.

skills.item_template: A claim about rational/irrational numbers to prove or disprove with justification. Constructed response (Part A verdict; Part B justification).

sample_items.stem: A student says 0.454545... is irrational because it repeats. Is the student correct? Justify.
sample_items.answer: No. 0.4545... repeats, so it is rational: 0.4545... = 45/99 = 5/11. Irrational numbers are non-repeating and non-terminating.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A repeating decimal equals a fraction, so it is rational -- the claim is false.

sample_items.stem: True or false: the product of two irrational numbers is always irrational. Justify.
sample_items.answer: False. √2 x √2 = 2, which is rational, so the product is not always irrational.

sample_items.stem: Is 0.1121231234... (a non-repeating pattern) rational or irrational? Justify.
sample_items.answer: Irrational. It has a pattern but no fixed block repeats, so it is non-terminating and non-repeating.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A pattern is not the same as a repeating block.

sample_items.stem: A student says the sum of a rational and an irrational number is always irrational. Correct? Justify.
sample_items.answer: Correct. If r is rational and i is irrational, and r + i were rational, then i = (r + i) - r would be rational (a difference of rationals), a contradiction. So r + i is irrational.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Proof by contradiction confirms the claim.

redirect_script.prompt: Don't judge by looks. Check the claim against the definitions, or find one counterexample: 0.4545... repeats but equals 5/11 (rational); √2 x √2 = 2 (rational).
redirect_script.praise: You justified with a definition or a counterexample -- that's real mathematical reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: A single example that shows a general claim is false, like √2 x √2 = 2 disproving 'irrational times irrational is always irrational.'
A number that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers; its decimal never terminates and never repeats.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for AI.QE.6 (rational and irrational numbers in algebra).

worked_example_script.text: Write the claim: 'every repeating decimal is irrational.'
Is that always true? Can you find a repeating decimal that is rational?
0.4545... = 5/11 is rational, so the claim is false -- one counterexample is enough.
If a student agrees with the claim, ask 'what does 0.4545... equal as a fraction?'
Your turn: is √2 x √2 rational or irrational?

practice_problems.stem: Is 0.333... rational or irrational?
What is √2 x √2?

practice_problems.answer: No -- 0.4545... = 5/11 is rational. Only non-repeating, non-terminating decimals are irrational.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: irrational times irrational is always irrational. Justify.
Alex judged a claim. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Alex wrote: '√2 x √2 must be irrational because both factors are irrational.'
practice_problems.answer: √2 x √2 = 2, which is rational. Two irrational numbers can multiply to a rational number, so the 'always' claim is false.

practice_problems.stem: Is 0.1121231234... (never repeating) rational or irrational? Justify.
practice_problems.answer: Irrational -- it never terminates and no fixed block repeats.
practice_problems.notes: A pattern is not a repeat.

practice_problems.stem: Write a true 'always' statement about rational numbers and justify it.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'The sum of two rational numbers is always rational,' because a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd, a ratio of integers.

practice_problems.stem: Give a counterexample to: 'the sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational.'

activities.title: Always? Prove It or Break It
activities.instructions:
1. Read Alex's claim that √2 x √2 is irrational because both factors are irrational.
2. Compute √2 x √2.
3. State whether the 'always' claim survives, and why.
4. Write the counterexample that breaks it.

content.worked_problem: Claim: the product of two irrational numbers is always irrational. Alex agreed.
content.error_step: Alex assumed the result from appearance instead of testing it.
content.why: √2 x √2 = 2 is rational -- a counterexample breaks the claim.

activities.title: Always True or Not Always True
materials: Card set of claims about rational/irrational numbers
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each claim card into 'Always true' or 'Not always true.'
2. For an 'Always true' card, state the definition that guarantees it.
3. For a 'Not always true' card, give a counterexample.
4. Debrief: what kinds of evidence prove a claim versus disprove one?

cards.text: The sum of two rational numbers is rational
The product of two irrational numbers is irrational
Every decimal that never ends is irrational

activities.title: Prove or Disprove Debate
materials: Claim cards about rational and irrational numbers
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a claim card and decide together: always true, or not?
2. If always true, state the definition that proves it; if not, produce a counterexample.
3. The group gives a thumbs up only if the justification is a definition or a real counterexample.
4. Debrief: why does one counterexample settle an 'always' claim?

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'is this claim always true?' builds the DOK-3 justification the top band asks for.
Journaling the definition-or-counterexample reasoning consolidates the argument in writing.
Studying a correct justification beside a flawed one targets the generalize-from-appearance error.

questioning_prompts: Is this claim always true, or can you break it with one example?
What definition would prove the claim?
What is a counterexample that disproves it?
Does 'never ends' mean the same as 'never repeats'?
Can two irrational numbers combine to a rational one?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student applies a surface rule instead of testing with a definition or counterexample.
misconception_redirects.say: Don't judge by looks. Check the claim against the definitions, or find one counterexample: 0.4545... repeats but equals 5/11 (rational); √2 x √2 = 2 (rational).
misconception_redirects.praise: You justified with a definition or a counterexample -- that's real mathematical reasoning.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student thinks one supporting example proves an 'always' claim.
misconception_redirects.say: One example can't prove 'always' -- but one counterexample disproves it. To prove it, use the definition for every case.
misconception_redirects.praise: You knew the difference between one example and a general proof.

quick_checks.look_for: False (0.4545... = 5/11). 'True' means 'endless' is still mistaken for irrational.
Rational (= 2). 'Irrational' means the student generalized from the factors' look.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S2 (classify numbers as rational or irrational, including square roots) -- the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, move up to S5 (find the irrational among tricky look-alikes) and S6 (analyze and justify a generalization). If they fail, drop to S1 (select the irrational numbers from an easy set) to see whether basic recognition is intact. The decimal-conversion strand -- S3 (convert a fraction to its decimal and classify it) and S4 (convert a repeating decimal to a fraction) -- branches off as a separate check, since a student can classify numbers yet still struggle to convert between fractions and decimals.
